title: Lesson 5C — Attack Methods and Mitigations
objective: Study-guide review — Day 5 — Threat Modeling, Monitoring, Hunting, and Incident Response: Lesson 5C — Attack Methods and Mitigations.

blocks.text: Input and Output Manipulation

The official source includes injection attacks such as SQL injection, command injection, LDAP injection, XPath injection, and related input/output manipulation. The general pattern is untrusted input influencing an interpreter, query, command, or output context.
Mitigation themes:
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "Vulnerabilities: Input and Output Manipulation".
Secure Coding and Patching
Secure coding reduces vulnerabilities before release. Patching reduces known vulnerabilities after release. Both are required, but they solve different timing problems.

rows: Improve secure coding standard and review process

blocks.text: Teaching cue: patching is reactive to known issues. Secure coding and assurance are proactive controls that reduce defect introduction. SecurityX scenarios often expect both: fix the current issue and improve the process that allowed it.
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "Mitigations: Secure Coding Practices" and "Patching".
XSS and SSRF
The official slides explicitly call out Cross-Site Scripting and Server-Side Request Forgery.

Cross-Site Scripting happens when an application allows untrusted content to execute in a user's browser context. Teach the decision cue: the attack abuses output rendered to a user, so mitigations focus on output encoding, input handling, content controls, and secure framework use.

Server-Side Request Forgery tricks a server-side application into making unauthorized requests. Teach the decision cue: the server becomes the requester, so mitigation reasoning must focus on validating destinations, limiting unintended outbound requests, and monitoring unexpected server-side request behavior.
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slide "Vulnerabilities: Input and Output Manipulation".
Memory and Execution Vulnerabilities

Memory and execution vulnerabilities can allow crashes, arbitrary code execution, privilege misuse, or control-flow manipulation. The official source groups them under known attack methods and associated mitigations. Teach high-level reasoning unless the source provides deeper implementation detail.
Mitigation themes:
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "Vulnerabilities: Memory and Execution Vulnerabilities".
Cryptographic Issues

Cryptographic attack methods include weak algorithms, poor key management, expired certificates, insecure protocol choices, or missing integrity protection. The Day 4 crypto concepts support this lesson; Day 5 asks students to analyze the vulnerability and recommend mitigation.
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "Vulnerabilities: Cryptographic Issues".
Configuration, Supply Chain, and External Dependencies

The official source includes system configuration/management and supply chain/external dependencies. These are high-value SecurityX topics because advanced practitioners must reason beyond a single application bug.
Mitigation themes:
Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "System Configuration and Management", "Supply Chain and External Dependencies".
Data Security and Management Controls

The official 5C lesson includes mitigations around data security and management. Connect this section back to Day 1 governance and Day 4 data states. Application-layer data controls reduce impact when attacks reach data-handling paths.
Controls:

items: Classify sensitive data before designing access.
Enforce least privilege for application and service accounts.
Mask or tokenize data where full values are not needed.
Encrypt data at rest and in transit where required.
Use DLP or monitoring where data movement must be controlled.

blocks.text: Source: CertMaster Study Lesson 5C; M05 slides "Mitigations: Data Security and Management".

cheatsheet: New feature accepts untrusted input: Secure coding, validation, review, testing
Known vulnerable library is deployed: Patch or upgrade dependency
Repeated injection flaws: Improve secure coding standard and review process
Emergency exploit against deployed system: Patch, mitigate, monitor, and validate
Unsupported software cannot be patched: Compensating controls and replacement plan
